utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I ask everyone who testifies in our language to pause between the sentences and to speak the sentences slowly so that they could be entered into the transcript. If you watch the transcript and when you see a translation stop, then you are free to begin. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I provided a statement that I see in front of me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7233 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the statement on the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page, please, so that the witness can confirm that it's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it in Serbian and in English. Yes, this is my signature in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This statement, does it accurately, faithfully, reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is faithfully rendered in brief, succinctly. This is the work of some five years of judicial work, the work in Republika Srpska, what could be accepted in this concise manner, and there were some documents attached that would accompany the statement, some briefs, some judgements, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today that were put to you when you were providing the statement, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this bundle under Rule 92 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're tendering 16 associated exhibits, two of which we would ask for permission to add to our 65 ter list. I think the Registry knows which 16 they are, but if you would like me to go through each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that you're not tendering any exhibits that were referred to in paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then para 22 will be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And are there any other associated exhibits that you are not tendering? Shall we take a look at 1D8676 and 1D8677, which are referred to in paragraph 24. I'm not sure if witness's -- witness has made a specific comment about the document, and I take it that the paragraph could be understood without these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly up to you, Mr. President, if you believe that it's not an essential part of the statement. We could either lead it live or dispense with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. If I could weigh in. I would prefer that -- my view is that the statement is more comprehensible with those judgements, 8676 and 8677, because they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you would like to leave them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And in case of 65 ter 2264 referred to in para 27, I take it that you are tendering only those articles referred to, not in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one other clarification is 65 ter 18996, referred to in paras 26 and 27. Are you tendering it separately or are you going to attach it to the pre-existing B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's already admitted as an exhibit, 82603, so we're not tendering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with respect to the remaining associated exhibits, Mr. Nicholls, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it there's understanding what exhibits are actually tendered, and then that can be sorted out later on. So shall we give the exhibit number for the Rule 92 ter statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D7233 will be Exhibit D2986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then other 14 associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should have said 16. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that will be the Defence Exhibit 3002. Thank you, Your Excellencies. Now I would like to read the summary of the statement of the president of the Supreme Military Court of Republika Srpska, Mr. Novak Todorovic. [In English] Novak Todorovic was the president of the Supreme Military Court during the war. He finished the military academy in Belgrade and law school in Sarajevo, where he passed his bar exam. During his career, he was aspirant at Military Court in Sarajevo and in a civil municipal and regional court in Sarajevo. He was an investigative judge of the Military Court in Sarajevo from 1966 to 1968. After that, he became Deputy Military Prosecutor. From 1982 to 1992, he had a law firm in Belgrade. He was also the ambassador of the B and H in India from 1998 to 2001. Novak Todorovic was appointed president of the Supreme Military Court in 1992. He was asked because there had been a problem establishing the military justice system. A number of officers who worked in the military prosecutor's office in Sarajevo left for Serbia when the war started, and the military courts and prosecutor's office needed to be urgently organised and there were no personnel. He was persuaded to take up this position and was appointed by the presidential decree. Supplies and staff were required, and many of the prosecutors hired were inexperienced. The military justice system also had to be established, and the regulations were based upon the Belgrade basic regulations. From then on, the court was slowly developed and the remaining positions were filled. The judges were tasked with preparing guidelines for criminal prosecution with special emphasis on the treatment of prisoners of war, observing the Geneva Conventions. As the war continued, the caseload increased. Dr. Karadzic insisted on the independence of the justice system. He agreed with Novak Todorovic that members of the prosecutor's office and judges should not be members of the SDS, and also insisted that the justice system had to be just and in accordance with the law and any deviation would be dealt with swiftly. Neither Dr. Karadzic nor anyone from the Presidency or from his office called to intervene in a case or called on someone's behalf. Novak Todorovic was completely independent in his work. There were no interventions or interference in his work from military or civilian authorities. Dr. Karadzic further requested that the judgements of the military justice system should be written or spoken about to make people aware of its existence and the need to obey the law. The military courts were governed by a number of different laws to control their work. The Republika Srpska president was responsible for the appointment of military judges and prosecutors. However, Novak Todorovic is not aware of the president rejecting any proposal. The courts could not act on anything without a request being made by the prosecutor, who was acting only on the basis of a criminal report made by either the civilian or military police. Investigations could be completed at the request of prosecution before an indictment is drawn up. The prosecutor had the ability to discontinue the process -- proceedings at any time and without requiring authority from the court. In Novak Djokovic's practice -- Novak Todorovic's practice, he did not encounter a single case involving Serbs accused of serious crimes being released from prison or detention to return to their original units, and he never spoke to anyone who may exert influence over him in this respect. Each case was treated fairly, no matter of the ethnicity of the victim or perpetrator. In one instance, Novak Todorovic recalls a Serb's sentence being increased from 12 to 14 years on appeal, whereas in another matter, the convictions against a large group of Muslims were quashed as the evidence was not clear or reliable. Muslims, Croats, and Serbs were all tried at the Military Court, and a number of Serbs were tried for serious crimes including rape and murder. No difference were made between victims of different ethnicities and witnesses of different ethnicities. Novak Todorovic recalls an appeal that was dismissed as the grounds were not strong enough as it relied upon the argument that the witness was Muslim and therefore her testimony was not reliable. All cases were documented and all matters launched during the war which had not been concluded continued after the war, including those against the Serbs. Novak Todorovic was aware that the Muslim side did not process serious crimes committed by the member of the BH Army against Serbian civilians. The Serbian judiciary gathered sufficient evidence about a number of Muslim perpetrators who lived in Muslim-controlled territory but were therefore inaccessible to Serbian law. Even after the perpetrators appeared on television they were not charged. Novak Todorovic does not consider Dr. Karadzic to have usurped the judiciary by placing the military system -- judicial system and prosecutor's office under his direct jurisdiction as this was a temporary measure until the final acceptance and the adoption of regulations which was completed in December 1993. The president was responsible for disciplinary offences and a number of crimes also qualified as disciplinary offences. Further, there was a rebellion of part of the VRS in Banja Luka at the time and the order was passed, and therefore the president would be aware that the military police were not functioning either and there was a danger of a military coup. There was no intention to usurp the powers of the courts demonstrated when Dr. Karadzic did not oppose the decision to relocate the military prosecutor's office to Zvornik and create distance between the judiciary and civilian and military authorities. [Interpretation] This is the brief summary of Mr. Novak Todorovic's statement. We don't have questions for Mr. Todorovic at this point. I apologise about Djokovic. He's number one in tennis, so he's always being talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Todorovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you have noted, we have admitted your evidence in chief in the form of written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. I wonder whether you had such system in your Military Court, but that's our system at the moment. You'll now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Julian Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we do so, could we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your kind understanding, Mr. Todorovic. In the meantime, Mr. Nicholls, I take it that those documents we discussed will be soon uploaded on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll assign them new numbers. Yes, and they will be assigned new numbers, I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, sorry for that interruption. During this war, at the time you were head of the VRS Military Court, do you agree with me that war crimes were committed on all sides, on all three sides?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the Military Court prosecuted Croat and Muslim soldiers for crimes committed against the Serb civilian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not have such examples, very few. I mean, I remember now and from what I can remember, 90 per cent of the cases were Serbian soldiers being tried because we were dealing with robberies, looting, property crimes, homicides, serious crimes, but we did not have jurisdiction other than the case that Mr. Karadzic mentioned. There was this group from Banja Luka which was sentenced by the first instance court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that you're not going to find -- we did not have access to, and we were not able to try the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me -- could you repeat your last sentence, please. The interpreters didn't hear you. It's probably my fault.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We could not try military personnel, because that is in the jurisdiction of the military courts for military crimes for those who were in Croatia or in the territory of the federation. We were more involved in trials of soldiers of Republika Srpska. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you and be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, line 24, it was not recorded that the witness said, "We returned that judgement and then in the end they were acquitted."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in the case of Kovacevic and others from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. I believe that was a case of armed rebellion, but let me continue. What I'm talking about is prosecutions under Article 142, war crimes against the civilian population. Do you remember that Article?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I'm familiar with the Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I know it -- what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the answer. I asked you if you remembered it and you said, "Of course." Now, I don't want to go through them, but in the Banja Luka Military Court, let's see if this refreshes your memory, in their register, that's P03607, I just looked quickly through it, not the whole thing, but I saw that there were records for war crimes under Article 142. Entry number 9, Jozo Baric, an HVO member. Number 55, Davnor Glasnovic [phoen], Croat, HVO member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, if you are going to hear the witness's response, why don't we show him the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I -- I'm just trying to spark his memory, Your Honour. I don't have that one loaded up. It's in a format that we can't show in English in e-court because it's so huge. At the moment we're still working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember if the Banja Luka Military Court prosecuted HVO members and Green Beret members for crimes under Article 142? If you don't remember, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall that. I do not. I would certainly have remembered it had a case like that come before the Supreme Military Court, because I was president of the Chamber in all appeal cases. Perhaps there may have been some such cases which had not reached the Supreme Court. Perhaps if we looked into the case file, we might be able to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me see if I understand your answer there. Are you saying you don't know what was going on in the Banja Luka Military Court unless the cases reached you on appeal? You're not aware of what the situation was in the Banja Luka Military Court in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about another case. Do you recall hearing at an time about the massacre of 80 civilians in Velagici on June 1st, 1992? That's Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Kljuc? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That doesn't ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, let's bring up a document, P03513, and what I'm going to show you now, sir, and put to you is the case we're going to look at, Amidzic and others, is the only time that the VRS Military Court prosecuted a VRS soldier for war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142. And I use the word "prosecute" rather loosely. Now, take a look at this, sir, if you could. Can you read the screen? Is it okay for you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It would be better if we could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This serves a request by the military prosecutor to an investigating judge to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And we can see --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page? We have six accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just as we're going, this is 8 March 19 --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Twelve; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. And it's 8 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll read it out, the paragraph at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else, page 3, perhaps, so that I can see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's stay here. All right. The bottom of page 2. On 1st of June, 1992, a group of 80 civilians were brought to the check-point in the village of Velagici - Kljuc - for identification, and then it continues on about how these 80 civilians were killed. For time, I don't want to go through all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you see at the top of the page, it was suggested that this was a war -- that these VRS soldiers be prosecuted for committing a war crime against the civilian population under Article 142, signed by Captain Zoran Babic. Take your time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What is the date of this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The date of this request, it's on page 1, 8 March 1993, for the crime that was committed on the 1st June of 1992. Now, having read the request for the investigation about this murder of 80 civilians by the VRS and the request for an investigation under Article 142, do you remember now whether you ever heard anything about this case?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Now I remember that since this is in 1993. I don't remember anything from 1992. But this probably involved the exhumation of a grave, where the victims were found in it. Deputy military prosecutor in Banja Luka requested an investigation against these people. Perhaps because an investigation could not be carried out and they were out of reach, nothing was done -- nothing much was done, because not even the first instance judgement was rendered, let alone hearing the case on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that was total speculation on your part, because this crime was not discovered by the finding of a mass grave. This crime was known about as it happened, immediately. I don't really have the time to go through all of the facts of this case, but I think I can show you something that will show you that your speculation there was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to P03614.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't think I'd have to show you this, but let's look at it. And while it's coming up, I'll just say for the record this is a document dated 12th of June, 1992, i.e., 11 days after the war crime, and it's a handwritten complaint about illegal detention from the accused in this case to General Talic, who you probably remember was commander of the 1st Krajina Corps. So take a look at that where they ask to be released, these suspects. Now, that shows you, doesn't it, that immediately or shortly after the crime, in fact, the suspects were brought into custody and were held in custody, because they're asking the corps commander to intervene to get them released; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention for the transcript. To release doesn't mean to set free. Release means let someone out, and to set free is a -- within the judicial remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a totally, totally, totally inappropriate intervention, I would say, Your Honour. To release, set free, we are talking about let them out of gaol, however you want to characterize it. That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, no, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is receiving that interpretation "to set them free," because it was simply being misinterpreted. It turns out as if the witness was supposed to discuss their release --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can clear this up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or rather their being freed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because the witness is able to read that letter, so let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah. [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I -- sorry, sorry?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Just want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One correction for the transcript, when I asked my question before the accused -- before Mr. Karadzic intervened, the witness said yes. That's what I heard on the transcript, he said "Da."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So let me ask the question again and you can explain.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The suspects were brought into custody at sometime shortly after the crime, and they asked the corps commander to have them released, set free, however you want to call it, that they not be in prison any longer; correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: This is probably true and accurate. Things probably developed that way. However, at that time, first of all, I was not in RS territory. Second of all, the courts were not up and running yet. It was at the beginning of the war still. This appeal -- or, actually complaint to General Talic, because they obviously asked the corps commander to be released. They were probably held in military detention, because the courts were still not operational at the time. I said that in my statement. I arrived in the summer of 1992, and the first courts began being established in that autumn. As of 1993, we were up and running. This was not a court case, and that's why it was not heard before the Supreme Military Court. That's why there was no trial judgement. It's still the beginning of the war. They were in some sort of military detention where they had been placed by their military commander, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well let me ask you this before we move on and --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As for the request for investigation, I see it was submitted in 1993 in order to have it investigated, and then nothing follows, meaning that there was no judgement, no one was sentenced. I don't know what happened. I presume that the prisoners were exchanged or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll -- you'll learn a little bit more about this case in the next couple questions, but let me ask you this as president of the Supreme Military Court: Even if the courts were not up and running, is the proper legal thing to do when -- when a group of soldiers have been arrested for killing 80 civilians, is the proper thing to do to just release them? Is that lawful in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 00904, please. Sorry, e-court page 14 of the English and 13 of the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is the 20th of July, 1993. The Military Court in Banja Luka. The military courts are up and running. By your testimony they have been since the previous September. And it's an order for detention, same case, Goran Amidzic and others for war crimes under Article 142, and you can see another provision I'm sure you remember, that it's mentioned is compulsory pursuant to Article 191, paragraph 1 on the Law on Criminal Procedures. So this is correct, isn't it? It's -- it's an order to impose detention --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This was a decision of the first instance Military Court in Banja Luka on detention against two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Two of the suspects.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I admit that, please, Your Honour? Or may I tender that, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Examine P6143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification, are we just tendering that page? It's a 77-page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just the order for detention which is two pages of English, one page of Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. That's 20th of July. Let's move forward nine days, P03616. This is -- while it's coming up, you remember Srboljub Jovicinac, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He wasn't young and inexperienced, was he? He was a good prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I always had my opinion concerning Jovicinac, but it's not relevant here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just take a quick look at this. It's a proposal 29 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He is addressing the Military Court asking to halt any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the military prosecutor is proposing to halt the investigations until further notice and to release two of the accused from custody, and I won't go into all the reasons now. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you didn't know anything about this before I showed you this document; right? Is that my understanding?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's 65 ter -- I thought this was an exhibit. 00904 again, please. E-court page 10 in English, 9 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, this is --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same day, 29 July 1993, an order terminating detention for the same two suspects and ordering their immediate release, signed by investigative judge Nikola Tomasevic.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The investigating judge. Since the prosecutor wanted the case to be dropped, the investigating judge agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he didn't need to, did he? That's in paragraph 14 of your statement. The judges do not need to follow the recommendation of the prosecutor to release; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in an interview, Srboljub Jovicinac agreed that this case and the release of these men and the stopping of the investigation represented a massive failure of justice. You would agree with that, wouldn't you, that what I've just shown you represents a massive failure of justice by the Military Court you were president of?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not aware of any details. The case did not reach the Supreme Court, as I've said. I simply don't know. I didn't take part in the proceedings, and there were many cases. There were four courts of first instance, and the Banja Luka one had a significant case load. I don't know. One would need to look into the reasons first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it definitely had a significant case load and if I have time I will go through some more of those cases with you. But I'm putting it to you that the case we've seen, Amidzic and others, was the first, the last, the only attempt at prosecution of VRS soldiers for war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142 for the entire war. Can you show me one other case?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were other cases, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Name one, please. Show me one.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In principle I don't remember names, but I recall a case from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me stop you one second and be very clear. I'm not trying to stop you from answering. I am not talking about prosecution for murder under Article 36, mass murder under Article 36. I'm talking about prosecutions for war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think -- well, I told you that in 99 per cent of the cases, the accused were members of the VRS, that is to say, military personnel who had committed certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to stop you --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The victims were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the proportion. I understand that, that in 99 per cent of the cases it was persons of Serb ethnicity who were prosecuted. I'm not asking you about that.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm asking you, and then I'll move on, if you can recall any other case in which the VRS Military Court during the war prosecuted Serb soldiers, VRS soldiers, for crimes -- for war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142. And just try to make it yes or no, if you remember any others or if you don't.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. We didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I tender that document, please, although I say I did think it was an exhibit, but I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit page 10 -- or shall we add it to the P6143.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be pages 10 to 11, please, Your Honour, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separately. Or shall we add those pages to the document we admitted today earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that makes sense. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we do that. Yes. Those pages will be added to Exhibit P6143.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, my last question on the Velagici massacre and case. I'll just put it to you that as far as we know in the OTP here, to this date nobody's been prosecuted for that crime. Do you know if anybody has?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The mass crime on Serbs, against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, the June 1st massacre of 80 civilians in Velagici, Goran Amidzic and others, the case we've been looking at. I'm putting it to you that, to this date, none of those accused who we saw write to General Talic to ask to be let go has been prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the case was never reopened, and it never reached the Supreme Court, meaning that there was no continuation in the proceedings. A court cannot try unless there is an indictment, much as the cases here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, can I clarify with you one thing. You referred to Article 36, murder and mass murder on the same Article. Is it your case that there were cases against Serb soldiers, VRS members, for committing these crimes against Muslim people, the killing of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you're asking were there cases of Serb soldiers for committing crimes of murder under Article 36 against Muslims and Croats, my case is that, yes, there were cases opened, investigated, and begun, but that none of them were concluded or properly prosecuted during the war unless the case involved Serb victims as well as Muslim or Croat victims. That's my case, that there were certainly cases brought under Article 36, but my case is that this was the only attempt to try cases -- a failed attempt to try Serb soldiers for a war crime and that all the other cases, even with multiple victims of civilians, if they started, were brought under Article 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to be clear, we have in our evidence Article 36 and 142. Otherwise, I'd like to have it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can bring up the Articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you check it later?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can bring up the Articles now. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 2264, please. Pages 69 of the English, 66 of the Serbian. And this is Article 142, war crimes against a civilian population. This is the 1990 Criminal Code of the SFRJ that was used at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admitted part of this Criminal Code as an associated exhibit. What Article is it then, Article 201 and 217, yes. So shall we add Article 36 and Article 142?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Article 36 is in a different document, Your Honour, which I can also bring up. This one would be Article 142, and I agree that it would be good to add it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll add Article 142. Yes, let's proceed, and I'd like you to tender, later on, the Article 36 you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just -- so I don't forget, I'll do it right away, Your Honour. It's -- 24617 is the 65 ter number. English page 22, Serbian page 24. And I'm sorry, I should say 24617A is a revised translation of Article 36. That's the one we should admit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I give explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, by all means, but could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned mass murder, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I meant was -- there's not an Article of that. Article 36 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Subsection (6).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was looking for without my glasses. Subsection (6) refers to two or more murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Todorovic. Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that it is not correct that there were no completed cases where the victims were of a different ethnicity. I'm just speaking off the top of my head, but I remember a case from the Bijeljina court for the rape of a Muslim woman. I remember a case of the killing of a Czech citizen from Grbavica. Then there were robberies. All these cases had their epilogue at the Supreme Court, and all the perpetrators were condemned. I remember an exhumation of a mass grave also, but I don't think that that was in Kljuc. It was somewhere in the Krajina where this Professor Stankovic came to do the autopsies, where the Serbs were in the mass grave. This was done. But as for specific cases, we adhered right from my arrival to a decision of the Assembly that, because there were no regulations of our own, we were to implement the Criminal Codes and the Law on Criminal Procedure of the SFRY, because that Yugoslav Criminal Law and Law on Criminal Procedure were codified and harmonised according to international law. Also, it included the provisions from the Geneva Conventions. War crimes were dealt with there, respecting the principle nullum crimen sine lege so we conducted our cases pursuant to that law. You could not adopt a regulation and then try somebody, but you had to apply the laws in effect at the time when the crime was done. So it's not that these crimes were not dealt with. As for war crimes, when nothing was processed, we didn't have any investigations other than some charges about what the corps did at the beginning of the war. There was some investigation conducted, but it wasn't completed, so we couldn't do anything there because there was no case that was initiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue will be brought up later on without doubt. Shall we admit this Article 36 as Exhibit P6144. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just for my planning, I think I have about 20 minutes more. I wonder if I could ask for another 15 to 20 minutes. If not, I'll have to adjust my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see how it evolves. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to go quickly through another part of your statement, paragraph 14. You said: "Persons accused of serious crimes which constitute a threat to society such as murder will be remanded in custody until the end of the trial. Even if the Prosecutor were to request a release from custody, in such cases the Court would be under no obligation to approve it." I put it to you that that is a completely false statement as it applies, for instance, to the Banja Luka Military Court. Now, one way to shorten this, if you'll agree with me that you have no idea whether or not the Banja Luka Military Court released persons charged with murder under Article 36 to go back to their units when the victims were Muslims, you don't know whether that was the case or not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't know what the practice was there. Okay. That will speed things up. In paragraph 19 you say: "In other words, if a Serb killed a Serb, he would have been sentenced to the same or similar crime as a Serb who killed a Muslim or a Croat for the same crime." I'm putting to you again, that's not -- that's not a true statement. That's not a correct statement as it applies to the Banja Luka Military Court and other military courts. Are you seriously saying that the sentences were the same for soldiers who killed other Serb soldiers as they were for Serb soldiers who killed Muslim or Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I am saying that, absolutely, seriously, and truthfully. I always abided by the principle that I was blind to ethnicity as far as a criminal was concerned. I was blind to religion or anything else. A crime is usually committed for some pathological reasons, out of some interest or some lowly motives, and in most cases, it's a person that would need to be isolated from society. So that we did not differentiate there, our judgements did have -- reflect this. We had stronger, stricter sentences. We would amend them or reverse them depending on the circumstances so that the practice in other military courts, those of first instance as well, were also shaped by our judgements. I don't know if there were any individual cases like this particular case where there was no investigation carried out even. That's something that I cannot know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just be clear. In your statement when you talk about these things, you keep -- you keep sort of referring to what you did and your impartiality. Let me try to be precise. Do you know whether, just for an example, other courts like the Banja Luka Military Court issued the same sentences for Serb soldiers who killed Muslim victims as they did for Serb soldiers who killed other Serb soldiers or Serb civilians? Are you asserting that those sentences were the same? I'm not talking just about what you did.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I assert that they were the same, and if you like, you would need to take all the cases into account. We can look at all the documents -- all the cases from all the military courts. We can make an analysis. There were many such cases, but I'm sure that you would come to the conclusion that the criteria were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, the -- we come to the exact opposite conclusion, sir, and I'll show you some examples. But in the rare, rare instance that a Serb was actually sentenced and served a sentence during the war for killing a Muslim or a Croat victim, if they even ever got to that sentence stage, it was invariably lower than for a similar crime. And I'm going to show you an illustration of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 05688A, please, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is a case you'll remember, because it reached your court, the case of Pero Marin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to need the English as well for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, this is dated 22nd of June, 1993, Military Court Banja Luka, same court that at the same time was dealing with the Velagici case. It's the case against Pero Marin, and to make it very brief, the facts of this case, which you'll see, are that it was a Serb soldier who was drunk, hitchhiking. A car didn't stop to pick him up, so out of anger he shot at the car and tragically killed a little Serb boy who was in the car. If you look at this judgement, you'll see that this man was held in detention throughout the hearing and was sentenced to 12 years in prison for one murder of a Serb boy.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: May I look at the other pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: -- of the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could please continue to page 2 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what I'll put it to you ... So what I'll put it to you is this shows the system working pretty well. A Serb soldier kills a Serb boy while he's drunk because he's angry. He's held in detention and then he's sentenced to 12 years. That's the way it should work. May I -- you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. The maximum sentence was 15 years for such a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that document, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, another case you'll recall is the Stankovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 05692, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the Stankovic case?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll show it to you. This is the same Banja Luka Military Court, 21st October 1993, and the facts of this case - I'll give you a chance to look at it, you can hopefully read it quickly - is that a Serb soldier, drunk and angry, walks through the town, murders a woman, a Muslim woman, with his machine-gun. That's on the bottom of page 1 of the English and should be on page 1 of yours. Keeps walking along, murders some other people with his machine-gun, and then seriously injuries two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we see in the English, thus he took the --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I look at the rest of the pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll just read this out where you're looking --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I just want to see the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But in summary, he took the lives of two persons and attempted to take the lives of two others. So that's Article 36(6), murder of two or more persons.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: May I also look at the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. We can continue through. And what you'll see there under "Sentence" is that he was sentenced to four years and six months in prison. We also see there that he was in custody from August 1992 to February 1993, in other words, six months and, in other words, not through the entire hearing as he should have been.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: May I look at the statement of reasons, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: And the next page, please. Because I just wanted to see what the criteria were and on what basis the court made its decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can I look at the next page, please. I am still not getting the last page or the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just while you're reading, you want to keep in mind that both of these judgements are by the same judge of the Banja Luka Military Court.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the name of the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Judge Svetozar Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on this last page, please, enlarge it. In the statement of reasons, this Judge Davidovic, I can see him state here because of the health of the -- or mental state and for other circumstances the sentence was reduced. We need to take into account the position of the -- I cannot see. One must also take into account the view expressed by the inhabitants of the village in question as members of all three ethnic groups. So I see that there are no elements to call for a heavier sentence. There are several mitigating circumstances - the remorse expressed by the accused, his family situation, the absence of previous convictions, and his good behaviour during the proceedings. This notwithstanding the sentence could not be milder because of the degree of public danger caused the serious consequences as well as for the sake of the -- of general prevention. The court rests assured that the aim of sentencing will be achieved by the sentence passed. I don't know if there was any appeal lodged, if the judgement was submitted to the Supreme Court, to us, for review. I don't know if the sentence is strict or not. We would need to look at the case files again, the findings of experts, and so on. There are no identical two crimes or two identical sets of circumstances. Each case is different, and it's very difficult to compare them and sentences are somewhere mild in some cases and in some cases they are strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah -- fine. But all these documents are in evidence. I'll put it to you that the principal difference in these two factors is that in one case, a drunken Serb soldier killed two Muslim civilians and severely wounded two others as he attempted to murder them, and in the other circumstance, the victim was a Serb boy. That's the main difference. And if we -- I'll try to do this without bringing it up, but we have in evidence P03633. That's another judgement on this same Stankovic which the Court has seen. See if you remember it. This man Stankovic didn't even serve his four year, six months' sentence until, less than a year later, he accidentally shot two Serb girls while carelessly handling his rifle. And then after he shot two Serb children by accident, he finally went to prison for eight years. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I seem to remember that vaguely. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that there were two sentences, but in the end, it was one sentence that was passed down for both of these things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I think I've been fairly efficient. The witness has clearly wanted to read quite a lot of the documents, which is fair enough. I would ask for another 15 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could just be heard on the relevance or necessity of this line of inquiry. As a Defence counsel, I somehow find that this procedure to be somewhat uncomfortable for a judge be having to explain acquittals. I can almost see Judge Meron sitting there being questioned by some prosecutor about Gotovina or other cases, and I'm not sure that it's productive to continue along this way. So if Mr. Nicholls has some other lines that he hasn't pursuant yet, perhaps he could tell you what they are and you could decide if they're necessary. But to simply ask a judge, the president of a court, to explain acquittals or lenient treatment, I think is of very low probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, they -- may I -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They have called this judge. I'm not concerned at how uncomfortable he may feel. They have called this judge and had -- and taken a statement from him saying that -- implying that throughout the system there was equal treatment, that the court was blind to ethnicity, and our position is that is blatantly false. And the way to expose that what is in this statement is not true is to show some specific examples, and the judge has been able to show that: I don't know about this, that's true. I don't have time to go through actually dozens of examples I have in here, but I don't think there's been anything unfair about my cross-examination, and I would prefer not to mention where I'm going to go next in the next 15 minutes. If you grant that to me. I can tell Your Honours it will be different, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I recall that Dr. Karadzic was frequently required to justify extensions of time for his cross-examination by explaining the areas that hadn't been covered. I think the Prosecution should have to live by those same standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break now, Mr. Nicholls, and you will have 15 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first may I tender 05692, the last document we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm not talking about the micro-level anymore, individual cases. We're kind of through with that small stuff. I want to try to look a little bit at the bigger picture. You say and it's shown in paragraph 37 of your statement and it's in the court files that -- you don't need to look it up. This is an easy one. The Supreme Military Court was located in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in Han Pijesak and later in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after the court, as you say, was dislocated to Zvornik to put more distance between the court and the Pale authorities and the Main Staff, did you live in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during trials while the court was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this dislocation moved the court farther away from the civilian and military authorities, but it moved it much closer, in fact, created zero distance between the seat of the Supreme Military Court of the VRS and the massive murder of Muslims in Zvornik municipality in July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. No, because those mass killings did not happen when we were moved to Zvornik from Han Pijesak. That happened in 1993 or 1994. That did not happen, and we didn't know about these murders even when they did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be very clear. Are you saying that in July 1995, that there were not mass murders in Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, in the sense that we didn't know about any mass murders, nor did we have any information or cases or indictments, nor did anybody consult us. We could not have had any knowledge about it. The relocation of the court was done because the premises had been too small. We had expanded as a court, and that's why we were moved to Zvornik. I personally commuted to Belgrade, but I lived there in a hotel --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which hotel?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: -- while I was working. Drina Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as you sit here today in this courtroom, do you contest that thousands of Muslim murders -- thousands of Muslim prisoners were murdered in Zvornik municipality after July 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: While I was in Zvornik and while I worked there, I didn't know anything about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. I'm asking today, as you sit here now, do you contest my statement that --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- that in July 19 --

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. You didn't understand me. I didn't know. In 1996 I was retired. I was removed from that post, and we didn't have any cases, and we had no official information. In fact, we didn't have any information about any murders. What you are asking me I learned about only from the media many years later when I was no longer there, when I was in Belgrade. Whether they really happened and what kind of murders, I still do not know today. It's not clear to me. I know chaos reigned. I know there was crimes perpetrated by all sides, but whether a genocide was perpetrated, I personally don't think so. But that there were crimes and killings of prisoners, I only learned later, and also from following proceedings in The Hague, on the internet, on television, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So as a citizen, just also a person living in Zvornik, you didn't know that thousands and thousands of Muslims were killed in Zvornik? Please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 24618, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because I don't have of time, this is a transcript of a television interview from PBS in the United States. It's dated January 25th, 1996. We go to page 2. It's not in your language, sir. I'll just read out your answer, see if you remember this interview. Again, January 25th, 1996. So six months after the murders that I say occurred. Colonel Novak Todorovic, when you were asked about these: "About Srebrenica I don't know anything exactly because we have nothing about Srebrenica in our court here, and in our courts in the first level, I know that we have nothing." And then you were asked: "Do you think it will be a possibility?" And you answered: "I don't know, really. I don't know. I hear that the international court in The Hague has something about that. If they give us we shall consider that case and where to go and to make sentences." So was -- your answer was truthful at least in the respect that the Military Court six months after the fall of Srebrenica was doing nothing to prosecute anybody for that crime?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What you have just put to me in the English language is true, and I believe it was some American television or perhaps the BBC reporters did come, and I enabled them to tour all military prisons, military courts, to take interviews, and of course they visited me at this Supreme Military Court, and what I said was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Just as this court cannot proceed without an indictment, I'm saying give me an indictment so I will do something. But we didn't have any indictments. We were a court, or we were trying to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. But you've also said that you personally didn't know anything about the murders, correct, until you learned about them from the media, right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I said even then that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P04397, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to take a quick look at about what the entire world, except for you, knew. This is not in your language, but it's a report from the 17th of July, 1995, in a British newspaper, "The Independent." And the title which is not subtle is "Bodies --"

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you enlarge this a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sure. It's called "Bodies Pile Up in Horror of Srebrenica." So that's what people in Birmingham knew the day after the Branjevo farm killings. And this refers to video that was shown in Belgrade of what we now know is the Kravica warehouse victims. So your testimony is that a taxi driver in Birmingham who is surprised -- read "The Independent" knew more about the Srebrenica killings than you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, thank you. I have several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, at that time were you reading "The Independent"?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did any of our newspapers provide any convincing information on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From your experience, did Western media in the past pass information that could or could not be believed?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course they did. Generally speaking, you can never trust newspapers, not now and not then. Although there existed decent and fair television crews, especially from the US who had their cameras also here when the Tribunal was established, and I believe they reported very fairly. And several BBC teams also visited. And it's not out of my great love for journalists but because I wanted the work of courts to be covered as widely as possible, all for the purpose of preventing crimes and putting criminals behind bars. And you insisted also that there be media coverage and that judgements be reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 37 of the LiveNote today, you were asked whether you knew or whether you found out that these people had been killed in Zvornik. When you learnt about it later, did you also learn that they had been killed in Zvornik itself?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. What I learned later from the media, from the press, but mainly from the trials broadcast from here in The Hague, are the mass graves in Srebrenica, not Zvornik. As far as I know, there were some criminals and paramilitaries in Zvornik at the very beginning of the war when complete chaos reigned, and it was the beginning of civil war. Early on, before I even assumed my post of president of the court, we insisted that all such detention centres and improvised prisons be abolished. Instead, we had three remand prisons, and at my insistence the wardens of these prisons who were professionals were returned to their jobs in Batkovici, in Bijeljina, and Tunjice near Banja Luka, and all these people knew their job so that nobody could be detained without a court order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm objecting as nonresponsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue. The question was about Srebrenica killing. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier today, esteemed Prosecutor Nicholls put to the Court his case, on page 24, lines 9 through 19, where he maintained that there was no case where a member of the VRS of Serb ethnicity had been tried for the crime of killing a Muslim unless they had also committed crimes against Serbs. I would like us to look now at one case that was finally judged before your Supreme Court, but let us start from the beginning. Prosecutor Nicholls said that these proceedings were never finalised and never reached a final judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D1757. D1757. This has already been admitted as a Defence exhibit. Thank you. Could we zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, could you tell us who is indicted here. What is the ethnicity of the perpetrator and the injured party?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it is the Military Prosecutor's Office Banja Luka. The last name is Vranjes, Miladin, son of Djuro, born in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is 13 April 1993, when he came to the house of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we remove the English version. The parties can see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something smudged here. Right. On 13 April 1993, at 1600 hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. What is the ethnicity of this Miladin Vranjes?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Now I don't see it on the screen. There were some personal details of his in the indictment. Son of Djuro and mother Dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of the injured party, Dzemil Abdic?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Looking for his son. Just let me see who he killed. Fired two bullets in the head. In the house. He came to the house of Dzemil Abdic, looking for his son Aso, and then upon not finding him he fired -- it is written something in -- there's something in -- handwritten.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next one, D1758.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of Camil -- Dzemil, sorry?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Dzemil or Camil, probably Muslims. But it's not written, I can't see it in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Todorovic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment again. I apologise for your inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we move into private -- no, just ... Yes. Let's move into private session and continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what decided the policy of keeping people in custody or allowing them to defend themselves when released?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The legal reasons are clearly defined. As for the basis for custody, if a serious crime is in question it depends on the highest possible sentence. There are other things such as influencing witnesses, danger to flee. If a person in question needs to be held in custody out of fear of influencing witnesses and the witnesses had already been interviewed, then that factor is removed, but there are a number of others, all of which are prescribed by law. The ethnicity of the victim had no bearing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours, and I'm sorry to interrupt. I just wanted to tell Mr. Karadzic that if he wants to, 65 ter 24626 is Article 191, the provisions on custody. Just if he finds that useful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following: Did anyone try to exert any influence over the length of custody in any one case?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any cases of your influence. I don't think you could have, because it was a court matter. There was no need to either, to exert any influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is missing in the question is whether I exerted any influence or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No one did, neither you nor anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is done in cases when the first accused or where there are multiple accused who are out of reach, whereas some other accused are in custody? We had some cases where we could see that some were provisionally released, whereas the first accused, Amidzic, was unavailable. Was it a serious breach if people are provisionally released until the first accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer the question. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, I think the judge can answer the questions without the leading. It began as a non-leading question, and then started asking if this is a serious breach if such and such occurs. I think he can just ask him what the procedures are without leading in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic now has understood, but please go on. Please carry on, Mr. Todorovic. You understood the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It would be a serious breach if a suspect is kept in -- held in custody even a day longer than necessary. As soon as there are reasons, grounds for custody, there are legal obligations on the part of the court, but custody is always re-examined. As soon as there are no reasons to keep someone in custody, that person should be released. If not all of the accused were accessible -- well, there are different matters to be raised in terms of whether they should be tried jointly or parts of the proceedings to be postponed, but there were such cases wherein no trial could be held because the accused were inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question: As regards the sentencing policy as well as their nature, the nature of sentences, what was the role of the president of the republic in that regard? Could he do anything?

utterances.speaker: NOVAK TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As regards sentencing policy, there was nothing he could do in my view. Regarding the judiciary in general and some general issues in that branch, well, in that case, yes, but he couldn't interfere in any cases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I have no further questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I followed your last answer, Mr. Todorovic, as to the question what role the president of the republic had in terms of sentencing when you answered in the last sentence: "Regarding the judiciary in general, and some general issues in that branch, well, in that case, yes." What did you mean by saying "yes"? The president of the republic had what role regarding the judiciary in general and some general issues in that branch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He could provide suggestions in terms of providing support to courts in terms of materiel, facilities, et cetera, but he could never provide any suggestions on sentencing policy. I as the president of the court could not provide any suggestions to my colleagues or to lower instance courts. Every Chamber had their direct access to their respective cases, and they could try according to their own professional conscience. I couldn't influence lower courts, for example, save through such cases which would eventually reach the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Todorovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to thank you as well as your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaurinovic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Kaurinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kaurinovic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from the accused, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaurinovic. Please continue -- please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kaurinovic, good day.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KAURINOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you so speak slowly and to pause between what I say and before you start speaking. Make pauses, because we're breaking the interpreters with our overlapping. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KAURINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
